en: Preface to the Newly Revised *Sifen Sengjieben*,
composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain.
In the second month of winter in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era, I revised and finalized this text at Fengde Temple on Mount Zhongnan.

Regarding the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, its preface states: "Since the practice of the *Prātimokṣa* first reached the Eastern Land (China), during the middle period of the Cao Wei dynasty, Dharmarakṣa first transmitted the *Karmavācanā*, yet the *Prātimokṣa* itself remained unclarified and incomplete.
It was only during the Yao Qin dynasty in the Guanzhong region that the extensive texts were translated. Dharma Master Jueming was the first to open the Vinaya section;
consequently, he produced this *Prātimokṣa* and appended it to the translations for copying and dissemination. During the reign of the Gao Qi dynasty, its propagation flourished greatly."

The Buddha-sun [shone] over the three regions, with more than two million companions of the Śākya lineage. Fashang served as the Great General Overseer (*dàtǒng*), coordinating and maintaining the whole.
The śramaṇa Huiguang was a figure of great renown among the clergy at that time; together with the high-ranking officials, he oversaw and managed this undertaking.

For one who seeks to restore the fundamental principles and rectify the afflictions of delusion, there is nothing that does not depend on the precepts for its establishment, and nothing that does not depend on the precepts for its propagation. Furthermore, seeking through the meaning [of the teachings], he compiled and gathered what had been lost or omitted.
A second copy was produced and widely circulated throughout the world; this is the version whose title page bears the words of homage (*namaskāra*).

During the Sui dynasty, the śramaṇa Fǎyuàn of Bingzhou disparaged the *Guāng* edition, claiming its doctrinal principles were flawed and its phrasing unsatisfactory. Consequently, later students relied upon it, yet it ultimately proved difficult to fully comprehend or validate.

Thereupon, [Fǎyuàn] took the Vinaya-piṭaka as his standard and transcribed the *Jièxīn* (The Heart of the Precepts) in its entirety. It spread throughout the regions of Fén and Jìn, where it was most highly esteemed and revered. Thus...

This refers to that which is titled "The Virtue of the Precepts" at the beginning of the original text. Having collated and compared the three versions against one another for their similarities and differences, I have integrated them all as supplements to the main scripture.

In extracting these principles and meanings, there is nothing that is not appropriate. For this reason, both the masters of former generations and the talents of later times have revered them without omission;

their intent lies in forgetting the trap (the means), not merely in the elegance of the phrasing. Yet in the world, there are those who are indolent in study and frivolously extravagant; they observe only superficially before following [their own whims].
Regarding the claim that "adherence to the same [view] as myself makes the difficult easy," if one listens differently, one realizes this statement is false.

Such partisan bias has become a custom that remains unpunished and unenlightened even now. Recently, during my spare time, I attempted to clarify this for you: according to what the *Prabhā* explains, when I say "I now recite the precepts" (*śīla*), it refers to the origin of the vow;
thus it is called the *Mokṣa*, and when one opens the Vinaya, it is explained as the *Mokṣa-śīla*. This vow originates from the beginning.

Regarding the precepts, Sengjie (Seng-jie) says "not returning," whereas the words transmitted by Faguang (Fa-guang) state "not abandoning. Upon examining the Vinaya commentaries, [it appears that] while [Sengjie] deviates from his own intent, he follows Faguang;
yet, if one grasps the underlying meaning and synthesizes the texts, they do not fail to return to purity. Such examples can serve to clarify their characteristics.

As for the virtue and essence of the precepts—truly clarifying concentration and wisdom, dissolving afflictions and quieting worldly affairs, transcending the world and transcending birth—one first enters the ford of inquiry here.

The returning boat reaches the shore; it is not opened without words, nor does it pass through without principle. When subtle discernment removes both conditions and simultaneously dispels the two attachments, one becomes vast and free from entanglement—whence could conflict arise?
I have thus caused my exposition to return to the fundamental source and follow the ancient tracks, pruning away the profuse and the overgrown, and repairing what was discordant and contentious.

My phrasing and reasoning are not obscure, and my explanations leave a trace. It is my hope that these words and deeds may be transmitted together, so that they may be understood by both the foolish and the wise.
Explanation: For those of us who have come from afar through the ages and have not yet attained this ultimate refuge, I have briefly composed this introductory preface.
This *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra) is derived from the Dharmaguptaka school.
I prostrate in homage to all Buddhas, And to the Dharma and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.
Now I shall expound the Vinaya rules so that the True Dharma may long endure. The precepts are like an ocean without shore; Like jewels, they are sought without satiety.
Those who wish to protect the noble wealth of the Dharma, Gather here and listen as I speak: I desire to eliminate the four offenses of expulsion (pārājika).
And having extinguished the offenses of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, obstructing the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules—O assembly, listen as I speak of the World-Honored Ones, the Great Virtuous Ones:
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni. May these Buddhas explain this matter for me.
I now wish to speak well; may all you worthy ones listen together.
Just as a person whose feet are injured is unable to travel anywhere, so it is with one who has violated the precepts.
If you wish to be born among gods or humans, and specifically if you wish to be born in the heavens or among men, you must always protect the feet of the precepts.
Do not allow it to be damaged; Like a driver entering a perilous path, The anxiety over a lost axle-pin or a broken shaft— the destruction of the precepts is likewise.
At the time of death, one harbors fear and dread; Just as a person looking at their own reflection experiences joy or sorrow based on beauty or ugliness, so it is with the recitation of the precepts:
preserving them whole brings joy, while violating them brings sorrow.
As when two armies engage in battle, The brave advance while the timid retreat, So it is with the recitation of the precepts:
From purity comes peace; from defilement, fear. Among those of the world, the king is supreme; Among all streams, the ocean is supreme; Among all stars, the moon is supreme;
Among all holy ones, the Buddha is supreme. And among all codes of discipline, [this is the most excellent].
The Precept Sūtra is supreme; the Tathāgata established these prohibitions.
Every half-month, the Saṃgha assembles to recite them. [If there are those who have not yet received full ordination, they are sent away. [If there are none, one says:
"There are no unordained persons in this assembly. Those bhikṣus who have not come must announce their *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purity).

[If someone says: "I announce the *chanda* [consent] for the sake of the *poṣadha*. Having announced the *chanda* and the purification (*viśuddhi*), if there is no one to convey the *chanda*, one should say: "In this assembly, there is no one who has announced the *chanda* or the purification.

[Question: "Who has sent a bhikṣuṇī to request instruction? [Answer: "In this assembly, there is no bhikṣuṇī who has come to request instruction. [Question: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall it perform? [Answer: "The *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*."

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today is the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight (or the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, or the fourteenth day; it is not fixed). The community of monks shall recite the Prātimokṣa.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience. The Saṃgha shall recite the Prātimokṣa in harmony.
Thus do I inform you, Venerable Sirs: I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa. All Bhikṣus should assemble in one place; you must listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
If there are those who have committed an offense, they should confess it; those without offense should remain silent. By your silence, Venerable Sirs, it shall be known that—
The purity of virtue: if others should question you, you should answer exactly as it is.

Thus, monks, if one among the assembly, even after three intervals, remembers having committed an offense but does not disclose it, one incurs the offense of intentional concealment (*saṃprajāna-mṛṣāvāda*).
The Buddha has taught that intentional concealment is a dharma that obstructs the path. That monk, knowing for himself that he has committed an offense, desires to seek purification.
One should confess. Through confession, there is peace and happiness.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard? (This is asked three times.
Since the venerable sirs remain silent, it is understood that you are pure in this matter. Thus shall this be held.
Venerable sirs, these four *pārājika* rules are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
The first is the rule against sexual misconduct:
If a bhikṣu, sharing the precepts and observing the same precepts, has not renounced them, nor does he admit to weakness in his observance of the precepts, yet commits an act of impurity—namely...
Even down to sharing with animals, this bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is not to live in community.
This is the second precept on stealing:
If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes an object that has not been given, with the intent to steal, it constitutes theft according to the value of what was not given.
Taking the Dharma: If one is seized by a king or a high minister, or bound, or driven out of the country, or killed, [and it is said], "You are a thief;
you are deluded; you have no knowledge," this bhikṣu is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in communion.
The Third Precept: Killing.
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being, provides a person with a weapon, praises death, encourages death, or says, "O man, [it would be better for you to die]."
"What is the use of this wretched life? It would be better to die than to live. Thinking thus, he employs various means to praise death, to extol death, and to earnestly urge death.
This bhikṣu is defeated; he is not to dwell in communion.
The Fourth Precept on Grave Falsehood:
If a bhikṣu, while actually possessing no such knowledge, claims of himself, "I have attained the state of a superior person;
I have entered the sublime dharma of noble wisdom; I know this; I see this," and at a later time—whether questioned or unasked—desires to clear himself...

Because it is for the sake of purification, this statement is made: "I truly did not know or see, yet I said I knew and I saw; this was a false, deceptive, and lying speech, except in the case of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and shall not live in communion. Venerable sirs, I have now recited the four *pārājika* dharmas.
If a bhikṣu commits even one of these dharmas, he may no longer live in communion with the bhikṣus as before.
The same applies to subsequent offenses. This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not live in communion [with the Saṃgha].
Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? (This is asked three times. Since the venerable ones are silent, they are pure in this matter.
Thus it shall be held.
Venerable sirs, these thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules originate from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month. Thus,
the rule regarding the emission of semen is first.
If a bhikṣu intentionally manipulates his own organ and emits semen, except in a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The second precept regarding touching a woman:
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, makes physical contact with a woman, or touches any part of her body, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa.
The third precept regarding coarse speech with a woman:
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, speaks coarse and lewd words of sexual desire to a woman, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The Fourth [Offense]: Praising One’s Own Person to a Woman in Order to Solicit Sexual Service.
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, in the presence of a woman, praises his own person, saying: "Sister, I practice the holy life and maintain the precepts;
I am diligent in cultivating wholesome dharmas. You may provide me with this service of sexual desire. To offer such service in this manner constitutes an offense.
The first and foremost: the Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The fifth precept concerning acting as a matchmaker:
If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between for both parties, conveying the intentions of a man to a woman and the intentions of a woman to a man. If...
For the purpose of performing wifely duties, or for the purpose of private intimacy, even for a mere moment, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The sixth precept concerning a cell exceeding the prescribed measure, not assigned by the Saṃgha and having no owner:

If a bhikṣu seeks to build a house for himself—having no owner and building it for his own sake—he must build it according to the proper measure. Regarding this, the measure is as follows: [text continues].
It should be twelve spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and seven spans wide at its inner width. He should lead the bhikṣus and designate the site;
they should designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions. If a bhikṣu designates a site that has difficulties or obstructions...
If one builds a dwelling for oneself, without an owner and for one's own use, and does not have the monks designate the site,
or if it exceeds the prescribed measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Seventh Precept: Regarding the Construction of a Large Dwelling with a Donor.
If a bhikṣu wishes to build a large dwelling for himself with a donor providing the materials, he must take other bhikṣus and designate the site.
They should designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from encroachments. If a bhikṣu [builds] on a site with difficulties or encroachments...
To build a large dwelling for oneself when there is a patron, without having another monk designate the site,
constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This is the eighth precept concerning groundless slander of others with a grave charge.
If a bhikṣu, being overcome by anger, slanders a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense with a groundless pārājika charge,
wishing to destroy that person’s pure conduct, and if at a later time— whether he is questioned or not—
he knows that this matter was spoken without basis and says, "I spoke those words because I was overcome by anger," it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
Chapter Nine: False Accusation Based on a Root.

If a bhikṣu, out of malice, seizes upon a fragment from a matter belonging to a different category and falsely accuses a bhikṣu who has not committed a pārājika offense [of having committed one], [he commits an offense].
If one slanders another with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense, desiring to destroy that person’s pure conduct,
and at a later time— whether questioned or not— knows that the accusation was taken from a fragment of a different matter and says,
"I spoke those words out of anger," it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Tenth Precept: Causing Schism in the Saṃgha despite Admonition.
If a bhikṣu desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, and through skillful means adopts the methods for causing such a schism, persisting in them and refusing to relinquish them.
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not accept the principles that lead to a schism and persist in holding them without relinquishing them.

Venerable sir, you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing without dispute, studying under the same teacher, like water and milk blending together; thus, within the Buddha’s Dharma, there will be increase and peace."

[The offense is] established. When that bhikṣu, being thus admonished, persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should be admonished up to three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it upon being admonished up to three times, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
The Eleventh Precept on Assisting in Dividing the Saṃgha against Admonition:
If a bhikṣu has other associates—whether one, two, three, or even countless numbers—and that bhikṣu says to those bhikṣus, "Venerable sirs, do not admonish this bhikṣu;
this bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya."
"Regarding what this bhikṣu has said, we rejoice and we approve. That bhikṣu should then admonish that bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable sir, do not speak thus, saying: "This bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya;
what this bhikṣu says, we rejoice in and we approve. For this bhikṣu does not speak according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya.'"
He should say to those monks: "Venerable sirs, do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṅgha. You should take pleasure in harmony;

let the venerable ones be in harmony with the Saṅgha, rejoicing and free from dispute, studying under the same teacher like water mixed with milk, so that there may be increase and a dwelling in peace within the Buddha’s Dharma.
If, when being thus admonished, those monks persist in their refusal to relinquish [their position], those monks...
The Buddha responded to the threefold admonition. Because he abandoned this matter, it was well; however, had he not abandoned it after the third admonition, it would have been a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This is the twelfth precept concerning defiling families, expulsion, slander, and disobeying the admonitions of the Saṃgha.
If a bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a village or a town and defiles the families there, committing evil deeds witnessed by all, the other bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, you have defiled the families and committed evil deeds, as witnessed and heard by all.
You should now depart from this village; you need not remain here. That bhikṣu should then say to those bhikṣus:
"Venerable sir, the Saṃgha now possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion.
There are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense as you, yet some are expelled while others are not. When the bhikṣus admonished him, saying, "Venerable sir, do not speak such words;

do not say that the Saṃgha possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, and that there are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense as you, yet some are expelled while others are not," [he replied:]
The Saṃgha is neither partial nor hostile; it is free from fear and delusion. "Venerable sir, you have defiled another's family and committed evil deeds;
this has been witnessed and heard by all. When that bhikṣu, being thus admonished, persists in his refusal to relinquish [his conduct], that bhikṣu should be admonished up to three times.
Because of this matter, he is to be admonished up to three times. If he relinquishes [the offense], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The thirteenth rule concerning a person of evil character who rejects the Saṃgha and defies admonition:

If a bhikṣu is of evil character and refuses to accept the words of others, and while the various bhikṣus are admonishing him in accordance with the Dharma regarding the rules of training, [he persists].
He does not accept words of admonition. "Venerable sirs, do not speak to me, whether it be good or bad;
nor will I speak to the venerable sirs, whether it be good or bad. Venerable sirs, please desist; do not admonish me repeatedly.
Other bhikṣus should speak to that bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, do not refuse words of admonition; you should accept words of admonition. Venerable sir, as..."
One should admonish the bhikṣus according to the Dharma; the bhikṣus, in turn, should likewise admonish the Venerable One according to the Dharma.
In this way, the community of the Buddha’s disciples attains increase as they admonish one another, instruct one another, and confess their faults to one another.

When a bhikṣu is thus being admonished, if he persists firmly and does not relinquish his position, that bhikṣu should be admonished up to three times so that he may relinquish that matter. If he relinquishes it by the third admonition, that is well. If he does not...
Regarding "abandoning": it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine offenses are committed at the first instance, while the remainder require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these dharmas and knowingly conceals it, he should be compelled to undergo *parivāsa*.
When the *parivāsa* has been completed, one should grant him the six-night *mānatva*. Once the *mānatva* has been performed, he should be granted rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
This bhikṣu’s offense should be cleared within an assembly of twenty monks; if there is even one person less, and the assembly does not number twenty, this bhikṣu’s offense cannot be removed.
O bhikṣus, you may also censure him; this is the proper time. Now, I ask: [Is it so?]
"Venerable sirs, are you pure in this matter? (This is asked three times. "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent.
Thus shall this matter be upheld."

Venerable sirs, these two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharma) are recited every half-month from within the Sūtra of the Precepts (Śīla-sūtra). Regarding the first indeterminate rule: if a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a location suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaks improper words; if he is accused by a trustworthy person who says, "I saw this bhikṣu sitting alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a location suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaking improper words"—if the bhikṣu admits to sitting alone with her in that secluded, concealed place, a location suitable for sexual intercourse, but denies speaking improper words, he should be dealt with according to one of two rules:

either the offense of intentional emission of semen (saṃghāvaśeṣa) or the offense of frivolous speech (duṣkṛta). This is the first indeterminate rule. Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a location suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaks improper words; if he is accused by a trustworthy person who says, "I saw this bhikṣu sitting alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a location suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaking improper words"—if the bhikṣu admits to both sitting alone with her in that secluded, concealed place, a location suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaking improper words, he should be dealt with according to one of two rules: either the offense of intentional emission of semen or the offense of frivolous speech. This is the second indeterminate rule. Venerable sirs, these two indeterminate rules have been recited. Now I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? Since there is silence, the Venerable Ones are pure in this matter. Thus do I understand.

It is said: There may be a female lay follower established in faith who, regarding each of three categories of offenses—whether a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*—declares that a seated monk has committed such an offense.
Regarding these three categories of offenses, he should be dealt with accordingly for each one: whether as a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*.
"Ti. As stated by a female lay follower who abides in faith, it should be dealt with according to the Dharma. This bhikṣu—this is called an undetermined rule (aniyata-dharma):
the undetermined rule regarding being in an open space."
If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in an exposed place, an unsuitable place for sexual intercourse, and speaks coarse and evil words,
and a faithful upāsikā states one or another of two dharmas against him— either a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If it is a *pāyattika*, the monk who was sitting there shall himself declare, "I have committed this offense.
Regarding these two rules, he should be dealt with accordingly, either for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*, as stated by the laywoman (*upāsikā*) who is trusted.
This bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma. This is called an *aniyata-dharma*.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the two *aniyata-dharmas*. I now ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this matter? (Ask three times.
Since the venerable sirs are silent, I consider you pure in this matter. Thus it shall be held.
Venerable sirs, these thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
The first is the rule concerning extra robes kept beyond the limit.

If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the kaṭhina cloth suspended, obtains extra robes, he may keep them for ten days without having made a formal act of relinquishment (apariśuddha-dāna).
If he exceeds this period, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
The Second Precept on Sleeping Separated from the Three Robes:
If a bhikṣu, after the robes have been completed and the kaṭhina period has ended, should sleep apart from any one of his three robes in a different location,
except by formal authorization (saṃgha-kamma) of the Saṃgha, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Third Precept on the Expectation of Robes:
If a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the kaṭhina has been relinquished, and he obtains an out-of-season robe, he may accept it if he has need of it.
Once received, it shall be quickly completed. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, one may keep it for up to one month in order to fulfill it.
If this period is exceeded, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Fourth Precept on Taking the Robe of a Non-Relative Nun:
If a bhikṣu takes the robe of a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange for another, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Fifth Precept on Causing a Non-Relative Nun to Wash Old Clothes:
If a bhikṣu causes a nun who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat old clothes, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Sixth Precept: Regarding the Prohibition Against Begging for Robes from Laypeople Who Are Not Relatives.
If a bhikṣu begs for a robe from a layman or a laywoman who is not a relative, except during the appropriate time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
What constitutes the "appropriate time"? It is when one's robes have been stolen, lost, burnt, or carried away by water; these are the appropriate times.
The Seventh Precept on Taking Excessive Robes:

If a bhikṣu has had his robes stolen, lost, burned, or carried away by water, and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative offers him as much robe-cloth as he desires, that bhikṣu should accept it with moderation.
If he accepts more than this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Pāyattika. The eighth precept concerning encouraging the increase of the price for robes:
If a householder or a householder’s wife prepares the price for a robe for a bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu has not previously accepted [the offer].
When invited to a layperson’s house for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, one says: "Excellent, layperson! Prepare such a robe and give it to me, for its sake.
If one obtains a robe [in this manner], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Ninth Precept: Exhorting Two Families to Increase the Price of Robes.

If two laymen or two laywomen provide the price for robes for a bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu, without having previously received an invitation to choose [the robes], goes to the houses of those two laypeople and speaks thus: "Excellent, layman! Prepare such [robes]..."
"Give me a robe; let us make one robe together for the sake of its beauty. If he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Tenth Precept on Exceeding the Limit by Urgently Seeking the Price of a Robe:
If a bhikṣu, whether a king, a great minister, a brahmin, a householder, or a housewife, sends a messenger to [a weaver]...
A bhikṣu sends the price for robes. That messenger goes to where the bhikṣu is and says, "Venerable sir, the price for robes has been sent;
you may accept it. The bhikṣu says, "It is not appropriate for me to accept this. I shall accept it when it is the proper time for robes and it is pure.
The messenger replies, "Venerable sir, do you have an attendant? The bhikṣu says, "Yes—whether he be a monastery servant or a lay devotee..."
"Upāsaka, this is the attendant for the bhikṣu. That messenger has gone to the attendant's place, given him the price for the robe, and returned to the bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable sir, I have already given the price for the robe to the attendant named so-and-so whom you designated.'"
"Venerable sir, know the time; go there, and you shall obtain a robe. A bhikṣu who needs a robe should go to the person in charge of robes.
If he obtains the robe after being reminded once, twice, or thrice, that is well.

If he does not obtain the robe, he should stand silently before him four, five, or six times to cause him to remember, so that he may obtain the robe; that is well. If he still does not obtain it beyond this..."
If he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If he does not obtain the robe, he should go to the place from which it came, either in person or by sending a messenger, and say:
"You previously sent a messenger with the price for a robe to be given to a certain bhikṣu;
that bhikṣu did not ultimately receive the robe. You should take it back so that it is not lost. This is the proper course of action.
The Eleventh Precept: Begging for Wild Silk Cotton to Make a Kāṣāya.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using wild silk cotton, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Twelfth Precept on Black Wool Bedding:
If a bhikṣu makes a bedding out of new, pure black wool from a ram, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Thirteenth Precept on White Wool and the Three Robes:
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he should use two parts of pure black wool, three parts of white, and four parts of variegated wool.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding without using two parts of pure black wool, three parts of white, and four parts of variegated wool...
Regarding bedding and seating (śayanāsana): it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The fourteenth precept concerning the three robes (*tricīvara*), which must be kept for at least six years:
if a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or seat, he should keep it for a full six years; if he uses it for less than six years without first relinquishing the old one, [he commits an offense].
Regarding the making of a new one: except by means of a formal monastic act (*saṃgha-kamma*), it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This is the fifteenth precept concerning the patching of sitting mats.
If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take a piece from an old one measuring one span in both length and width and sew it onto the new one.

In order to change its color: if a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat and does not take a piece from an old one measuring at least one span in length and breadth to be inserted into it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Sixteenth Precept on Carrying Wool Beyond the Limit:
If a bhikṣu obtains wool while traveling on a road and requires it, he may take it. If there is no one to carry it for him, he may carry it himself for a distance of three yojanas.
If he exceeds this distance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Seventeenth Precept on Having an Unrelated Bhikṣuṇī Wash, Dye, or Card Wool:
If a bhikṣu has an unrelated bhikṣuṇī wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Eighteenth Precept on Keeping Money and Precious Things:
If a bhikṣu receives gold or silver with his own hands, or money, or instructs another to take it, or verbally agrees to receive it,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Nineteenth Precept on Trading Jewels:
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. The Twentieth Precept on Buying and Selling:
[If a bhikṣu engages in buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.]
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The twenty-first precept concerning the limit for keeping an extra bowl:
If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl, he may keep it for up to ten days provided it has not been formally dedicated (*apariṇata*). If he exceeds this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Pāyattika. The twenty-second precept on begging for alms-bowls:
If a bhikṣu possesses an alms-bowl that has fewer than five patches and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This is a *pāyattika*. That bhikṣu must go before the Saṃgha and relinquish that bowl. It shall be passed around until the lowest-ranking bowl is obtained;
he should be given this and told to keep it until it breaks. This is the proper procedure.
The Twenty-third Precept on Begging for Thread and Having an Unrelated Weaver Weave Cloth:
If a bhikṣu begs for thread himself and has an unrelated weaver weave it into a robe,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Twenty-fourth Precept: Admonishing the Weaver to Increase the Thread of the Robe.
If a bhikṣu has a householder or a householder’s wife employ a weaver to weave a robe for that bhikṣu, that bhikṣu...
Without having previously accepted an invitation for a formal robe-offering, he goes to a weaver and says: "This robe is being made for me;
you should weave it with the utmost care, making it wide, long, sturdy, well-finished, and beautiful. I shall give you the price. Thus, that bhikṣu provides the price for the robe.
If one obtains a robe worth even a single meal [in exchange for it], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The twenty-fifth rule concerning the confiscation of robes:
If a bhikṣu has previously given a robe to another bhikṣu, and later, out of anger, either takes it back himself or causes another to take it back, this is a [fault].
The Buddha replied, "The robe must be returned. If one takes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The twenty-sixth precept concerning the seven-day limit for keeping medicinal substances:
If a bhikṣu is ill and keeps ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar as medicine, he may consume them for up to seven days. If he exceeds this limit, [it is an offense].

[If a monk] seeks a rain-bath robe before [the end of the first month of summer] or uses it before [the middle of the second month], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. This is the twenty-seventh rule concerning seeking and using the rain-bath robe too early.
If a monk has one month remaining of the spring season, he should seek a rain-bath robe; he should use it for bathing during the [subsequent] half-month. If a monk...

[The Buddha said: "Kauṇḍinya, one month before the spring [retreat], one may seek a robe for bathing during the rains; one who uses it half a month before [the end of the period] commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This is the twenty-eighth precept concerning receiving an urgent gift of cloth (*ātyayikacīvara*) before the time and keeping it after the time has passed.
If a bhikṣu, when less than ten days remain of the three-month summer retreat, receives an urgent gift of cloth, he should accept it until [the end of the] robe season."
It should be kept for that duration; if it exceeds this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The twenty-ninth rule concerning the separation of robes in a wilderness area during times of difficulty:
If a bhikṣu has completed the three-month summer retreat on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, and [the place is] remote...
There is a case where there is doubt, fear, or apprehension regarding a dangerous place. If a bhikṣu dwells in such a place and leaves any one of his three robes behind in a village dwelling,
and due to some necessary business he stays apart from that robe for up to six nights— if he exceeds this limit,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Thirtieth Precept on Diverting Property Belonging to the Sangha to One’s Own Use:
If a bhikṣu knows that another intends to give property to the Saṅgha, yet diverts it for his own use, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Venerable sirs, I have recited the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas. Now I ask the venerable sirs:
Are you pure in this matter? (Ask three times. Since the venerable sirs are silent, they are pure in this matter. Thus shall this be held.
Venerable sirs, these ninety *pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
First is the rule concerning minor forgetfulness of speech:
If a bhikṣu knowingly forgets to speak [the truth], it is a *pāyattika*.
The Second Precept on Reviling:
If a bhikṣu uses speech that disparages another by way of their lineage, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Third Precept on Divisive Speech.
If a bhikṣu engages in double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika.
The fourth precept concerning sleeping with women:
if a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
The Fifth Precept on Staying Overnight with One Who Has Not Received Full Ordination:
If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received the full precepts, exceeding two nights and reaching a third night, it is a pāyattika offense.
The sixth [offense]: Reciting the precepts together with one who is not fully ordained.
If a bhikṣu recites the precepts together with a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika. The seventh [offense]: Speaking of a grave offense to one who is not fully ordained.
If a bhikṣu speaks of a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) to a person who is not fully ordained, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to one who has not received full ordination,
except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
The eighth [offense]: speaking of the superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to one who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If a bhikṣu speaks of the superhuman states to a person who has not received full ordination, saying, "I know this; I have seen this."
If one speaks of this to one who sees and knows the truth, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Ninth Precept on Speaking Dharma to Women Beyond the Limit:
If a bhikṣu speaks the Dharma to a woman beyond five or six words, except when a man of intelligence is present, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Tenth Precept on Digging the Earth:
If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika offense. The Eleventh Precept on Destroying Living Seeds:
[If a bhikṣu destroys seeds or plants that have life, it is a pāyattika offense.]
If a bhikṣu destroys a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika.
The twelfth precept concerning frivolous speech of body and mouth:
if a bhikṣu speaks falsely or evasively to vex the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
Thirteenth Precept on Scolding the Monastic Officials:
If a bhikṣu scolds or reviles a monastic official, it is a pāyattika offense. Fourteenth Precept on Spreading Monastic Property Outdoors:
[If a bhikṣu spreads out monastic property outdoors...]
If a bhikṣu takes a monastic rope bed, wooden bed, bedding, or sitting mat, and spreads it out himself on an open space, or instructs another to spread it out,
and then departs without either putting it away himself or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Fifteenth Precept on Concealing Items Placed in a Monastery:
If a bhikṣu, within a monastic dwelling, spreads out bedding or cushions belonging to the Saṃgha—whether spreading them himself or instructing another to do so—[and then conceals them].
Whether sitting or lying down, if one leaves that place and does not pick it up oneself, nor instructs another to pick it up, it is a *pāyattika*.
This is the sixteenth precept on forced spreading.
If a bhikṣu, knowing beforehand that a bhikṣu already occupies a dwelling, arrives later and forcibly spreads bedding there to stay...
While staying there, he thinks to himself: "If they find it cramped, they will naturally avoid me and leave.
If one acts on such a pretext and not otherwise, and it is not due to a matter of proper decorum, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The Seventeenth Precept on Expelling Others from the Monastery:
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure toward another bhikṣu, personally expels him from within a monastery dwelling,
or instructs another to expel him, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Eighteenth Precept: Regarding Sitting or Lying on a Bed with Detachable Legs.
If a bhikṣu, in a monastic dwelling or on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sits or lies upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with detachable legs, [he commits an offense].
Pāyattika. The nineteenth precept regarding water containing insects:
If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains insects, uses it himself to sprinkle on mud or grass, or instructs another to do so, it is a pāyattika.
[The twentieth precept on the covering of a roof beyond three layers:
If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, and personally directs the assignment of the door-leaves, windows, and various decorative fittings for the roofing and thatching.
[The rule regarding] the second and third joints: if one exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika*.
The twenty-first [offense]: teaching the nuns without authorization.
If a bhikṣu teaches the bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Twenty-second Precept: Teaching the Dharma to Nuns until Sunset.
If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Twenty-third Precept on Rebuking Those Who Instruct Nuns:
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Those bhikṣus instruct nuns for the sake of food and drink," it is a pāyattika.
The Twenty-fourth Rule: Regarding Giving Robes to a Nun Who Is Not a Relative.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for goods, it is a pāyattika offense.
The twenty-fifth precept concerning making robes for a nun who is not a relative:
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Twenty-sixth Precept on Sitting in Seclusion with a Nun:
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded, concealed place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense.
The twenty-seventh precept on traveling with a nun:
If a bhikṣu agrees to travel along the same path with a bhikṣuṇī, even as far as a village, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to when there is suspicion or fear regarding the journey; these are the exceptions.
The twenty-eighth precept concerning traveling in the same boat with a bhikṣuṇī:
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment to travel in the same boat as a bhikṣuṇī, whether going upstream or downstream—
except in the case of crossing directly across— a pāyattika offense is committed.
The Twenty-ninth Precept: Eating Food Procured through the Praise of a Bhikṣuṇī.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the cause of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, eats it—except when the donor had prior intention—this is a pāyattika offense.
The thirtieth precept concerning traveling together with a woman:
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment to travel along the same road with a woman, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika offense.
31. The Rule on Receiving More Than One Meal at a Single Place:
If a place provides a single meal, a monk who is not ill may accept it; if he accepts more than that, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Thirty-Second Precept on Successive Eating:
If a bhikṣu eats successively, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense. The appropriate times are: when one is ill, and when robes are being offered.
When making robes, this is the proper time.
Regarding the thirty-third precept on eating in a group apart from others:
If a bhikṣu eats in a group apart from others, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense. "Other times" refers to the time of illness and the time of receiving robes.
When making robes, when traveling on a journey, when traveling by boat, during a great assembly, or when receiving food from śramaṇas—these are the proper times.
This is the thirty-fourth precept concerning taking food from a newlywed bride or a merchant.
If a bhikṣu goes to the house of a donor and they earnestly invite him with cakes, parched flour, or rice, and the bhikṣu requires it, he should accept two [mouthfuls].
One may accept three bowls. Having taken them, one should bring them inside at the proper time and distribute them to other bhikṣus as food.
If a bhikṣu, when not ill, accepts more than two or three bowls, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Thirty-fifth Precept on Eating to Satiety:
If a bhikṣu has finished his meal and subsequently accepts an invitation to eat more, yet does not perform the ritual of "remaining food" (atirittakaraṇa) before eating again,
it is a pāyattika offense.
The Thirty-sixth Precept on Exhorting Another to Eat Until Satiated:
If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has already finished eating, yet, upon being invited, he persistently requests and offers food, saying, "Venerable sir,
please take this food," and does so for no other reason than the desire to cause the other to commit an offense, it is a *pāyantika*.
Pāyattika. The thirty-seventh precept on eating at improper times:
If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.
The thirty-eighth precept concerning eating leftover food from the previous day:
If a bhikṣu eats food that has been left over overnight, it is a pāyattika offense. The thirty-ninth precept concerning not accepting food:
[If a bhikṣu eats food that was not formally offered to him, it is a pāyattika offense.]
If a bhikṣu places food or medicine into his mouth without having received it [from another], except for water and tooth-sticks, it is a pāyattika.
The fortieth precept concerning seeking fine food:
If a bhikṣu obtains excellent food—such as milk, curd, fish, or meat—and being without illness, seeks it for himself, it is a pāyattika.
Section 41:
The Precept on Giving Food with One’s Own Hand to Non-Buddhists.
If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to male or female non-Buddhists, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Forty-second Precept: Entering a Village Without Informing a Fellow Benefactor.
If a bhikṣu, having previously accepted an invitation, goes to another house before or after the meal without informing another bhikṣu—except at other times—it is a pāyattika.
"Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of making robes, or the time of receiving robes. This is it.
The forty-third precept on sitting forcefully in a family home where food is being served:
If a bhikṣu sits down forcefully in a family home where there is treasure, it is a pāyattika offense.
The forty-fourth precept: Sitting in a secluded place with a woman.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a woman while there is wealth present in the house of a lay family, it is a pāyattika offense.
The forty-fifth precept: Sitting alone with a woman. [If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman, it is a pāyattika offense.]
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open space, it is a pāyattika.
This is the forty-sixth precept concerning expelling another from a village.
If a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus: "Venerable sirs, come together to the village; I shall give you food."
That bhikṣu ultimately does not instruct the other bhikṣu to give him food, but says to him: "Go away!
I do not enjoy sitting or speaking with you; I enjoy sitting and speaking alone. If he dismisses him for this reason and by no other means, [it constitutes an offense].
Pāyattika. The forty-seventh precept concerning the acceptance of medicinal invitations for more than four months:

If a bhikṣu is invited to receive medicine for four months, a bhikṣu who is not ill may accept it; if he accepts it for longer than that, except in the case of a regular invitation, he commits an offense.
To invite [a monk] again, or to invite him for his entire life, constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the forty-eighth precept on observing the army:
if a bhikṣu goes to observe a military array, except when there is a specific reason, it is a *pāyattika*.
The forty-ninth precept regarding staying in an army beyond the limit:
If a bhikṣu, having a legitimate reason, goes to an army and stays for more than two nights—reaching a third night—it is a pāyattika offense.
The Fiftieth Precept: Regarding the Prohibition Against Observing Armies in Battle.

If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two or three nights, or observes military formations and combat, or observes the strength of the troops, elephants, and horses on patrol, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Fifty-first Pāyattika: The Precept Against Drinking Alcohol.
If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika.
The Fifty-second Pāyattika: The Precept Against Sporting in Water.
If a bhikṣu plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.
The fifty-third precept on tickling:
if a bhikṣu tickles another, it is a pāyattika.
The fifty-fourth precept: Refusing Counsel.
If a bhikṣu refuses counsel, it is a pāyattika offense. The fifty-fifth precept: Frightening a Bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣu frightens another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu causes another bhikṣu to be terrified, it is a pāyattika.
This is the fifty-sixth rule concerning bathing once every half-month during the secular period;
a bhikṣu who is not ill should observe this. If he exceeds this limit, except for other permitted times, it is a [pāyattika].
Pāyattika. The exceptions are: during the heat, during illness, during work, during wind, during rain, and when traveling from afar; these are the [permissible] times.
The Fifty-Seventh Precept on Kindling a Fire in an Open Space:
If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, kindles a fire in an open space for the purpose of warming his body—whether he kindles it himself or instructs another to do so.
Except in cases of urgent necessity, this is a *pāyattika*.
The fifty-eighth precept concerning the concealing of another’s robes, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case:
If a bhikṣu conceals the robes, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case of another bhikṣu—whether concealing them himself or instructing another to conceal them—[he commits an offense].
Down to one who takes it in jest, it is a *pāyattika*.
The fifty-ninth precept: Regarding the rule against taking what has been formally offered without being told.
If a bhikṣu takes the robe of a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī that has been formally offered as a pure gift (*śuddhaka-datta*).
If one wears [a garment] without asking the owner's permission, it is a *pāyattika*.
This is the sixtieth precept concerning new garments.
If a bhikṣu obtains a new garment, he must apply one of three types of dyed colors to ruin its original appearance: blue, black, or madder-brown. If a bhikṣu...
If one obtains a new robe and does not dye it with one of the three types of discoloring colors—blue, black, or madder—the wearer of that new robe commits a *pāyattika* offense.
This concludes the sixty-first precept: the prohibition against taking the life of an animal.
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
The sixty-second precept concerning drinking water containing insects:
If a bhikṣu knows that water contains insects and drinks or uses it, it is a pāyattika.
The sixty-third precept on causing distress to a bhikṣu:
If a bhikṣu intentionally causes another bhikṣu distress, even for a brief moment so that he is unhappy, it is a pāyattika.
The sixty-fourth precept on concealing the grave offenses of others:
If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense and conceals it, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the sixth and fifteenth [rules] concerning those whose years do not yet fulfill the requirement for ordination:
When one has completed twenty years, one should be granted the full precepts (upasampadā).

If a bhikṣu knows that a person is less than twenty years of age and nevertheless grants them the full precepts, this person does not obtain the precepts; the other bhikṣus may censure him for his folly. This is a pāyattika offense.
The sixty-sixth precept on inciting disputes:
If a bhikṣu knows that a matter concerning one of the four types of disputes has been settled according to the Dharma, yet later raises it again, it is a pāyattika.
The sixty-seventh precept on traveling with thieves:
If a bhikṣu knows someone to be a companion of thieves and agrees to travel together with them, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika.
The Sixty-eighth Precept: Regarding Wrong Views and Disregarding Admonition.
If a bhikṣu speaks thus: "I know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha—that the practice of sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path."
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, do not speak such words. Do not slander the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One;
the Blessed One does not speak thus. By means of countless skillful methods, the Blessed One has declared that engaging in sexual misconduct is a dharma that obstructs the path.
When that bhikṣu is thus being admonished, if he persists and does not relinquish his position, that bhikṣu should...
Up to three admonitions. If he relinquishes this matter, it is well; if he does not relinquish it after the third admonition, it is a *pāyattika*.
This is the sixty-ninth precept concerning formal accusation (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*).
If a bhikṣu knows that such a person has not had the formal act performed and does not relinquish such a wrong view, yet provides him with [necessities]...
If one performs formal acts (kamma) together with him, stays overnight with him, or converses with him, it is a pāyattika.
This is the seventieth precept concerning the expulsion of a śrāmaṇera.
If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has spoken thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not... [it is a pāyattika].
Regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path: that bhikṣu should say this to the śrāmaṇera, "Do not speak such words.
Do not slander the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One; the Blessed One does not speak thus.

Śrāmaṇera, the Blessed One has, by means of countless skillful methods, declared that the practice of sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path. If, when the śrāmaṇera is thus admonished, he persists and does not relinquish his position...

The Seventy-first Precept on Refusing Instruction:

Seventy-fifth: The Precept on Not Giving Consent.
If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is conducting its affairs, departs without having given his consent, it is a pāyattika offense.
Seventy-sixth: The Precept on Regretting Having Given Consent.
If a bhikṣu, having already given his consent (*chanda*), subsequently revokes it, he commits a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that other bhikṣus are quarreling, listens to their words and then reports them to those [involved], he commits a *pāyattika*.

One must not burn corpses within four paces of a stupa; this should be studied.
One must not burn corpses around the four sides of a stūpa so that the foul odor enters it;
this is a training rule. One must train thus. Regarding the seventy-third precept:
one must not carry a corpse’s clothing or bed beneath a stūpa, except for those items that have been washed, dyed, or perfumed; this is a training rule. One must train thus.
The seventy-fourth precept concerning defecating or urinating beneath a stūpa:
One must not defecate or urinate beneath a stūpa; this is how one should train.
The seventy-fifth precept concerning defecating or urinating toward a stūpa: [One must not do so]; this is how one should train.
One must not defecate or urinate facing a stūpa; this is a training rule that should be observed.
(Rule 76) One must not defecate or urinate within four paces of a stūpa so as to allow foul odors to enter; this is a training rule that should be observed.
Precept 77: Carrying an Image of the Buddha to the Place of Defecation or Urination.
One must not carry an image of the Buddha to the place of defecation or urination. This should be studied.
Precept 78: Chewing Tooth-sticks Beneath a Stūpa.
One must not chew tooth-sticks beneath a stūpa; this is a training to be observed.
One must not chew tooth-sticks facing a stūpa;
this is the seventy-ninth precept, a training to be observed.
The Eightieth Precept: While circumambulating the four sides of a stūpa, one must not chew tooth-sticks.
One should train in this. The Eighty-first Precept: One must not discharge snot or saliva beneath a stūpa. One should train in this.
One must not spit or sneeze beneath a stūpa; this is how one should train.
This is the eighty-second precept:
one must not spit or sneeze toward a stūpa; this is how one should train.
Precept Eighty-Three: One must not spit or discharge saliva while circumambulating the four sides of a stūpa;
this should be studied. Precept Eighty-Four:
One must not extend one’s legs toward a stūpa; this should be studied.
One must not sit with one's legs extended toward a stupa;
this is how one should train. This is the eighty-fifth precept:
One must not occupy an upper room while placing the Buddha’s image in a lower room; this is how one should train.
The eighty-sixth precept: One should not preach the Dharma while standing to someone who is seated, except when ill; this is how one should train. The eighty-seventh precept:
One should not preach the Dharma while sitting to someone who is lying down; this is how one should train.
One should train oneself thus: "When another is lying down and I am sitting, I must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
This is the eighty-eighth precept. One should train oneself thus:
"When another is seated and I am not seated, I must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness. This is the eighty-ninth precept.
Precept 89: One who is seated on a high seat must not preach the Dharma to one who is seated on a lower seat, except in the case of illness. This is a training to be observed.
Ninety: One should train oneself thus:
when another person is walking ahead and one is walking behind, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
Ninety-first: When one is walking on a high path and another is walking on a lower path, one must not preach the Dharma or the precepts to them, except in the case of illness.
This is how one should train.
Precept Ninety-two: When one is on the road and another is not on the road, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness. This is how one should train.
Precept Ninety-three: Walking on the road while holding hands. This is how one should train.
One should train oneself: "I shall not walk along a road holding hands.
This is the ninety-fourth precept. One should train oneself:
"I shall not climb a tree higher than the height of a person, except when there is a specific reason. This is the ninety-fifth precept.
Precept Ninety-Five: Carrying a Staff and a Strainer Bag.
One must not carry a strainer bag containing an alms bowl and thread it onto the head of a staff, then place it upon one’s shoulder while walking. This is how one should train. Precept Ninety-Six:
Preaching the Dharma While Holding a Staff. One must not preach the Dharma while holding a staff. This is how one should train.
One should train oneself thus: "If a person holds a staff, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
This is the ninety-seventh precept: one should train oneself thus:
"If a person holds a sword, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness."
Precept 98: One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a spear, except when they are ill; this is a training rule. Precept 99:
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a sword; this is a training rule.
One should train oneself: "I shall not preach the Dharma to a person holding a sword, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: "I shall not preach the Dharma to a person holding a parasol, except when they are ill. This is the hundredth precept concerning those who hold a parasol.

This is the Sūtra on the Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata Kanakamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Guard well your speech, purify your own mind, and commit no evil with the body;

This is the teaching of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, given during the twelve years [following his enlightenment].
The monks who have no worldly affairs shall recite this precept-sūtra.

The wise who diligently guard the precepts, Whose purity of precepts brings forth wisdom, Shall attain the foremost path, Just as the Buddhas of the past did.
